content.html:
Module 2›Chapter 1›The Arista EOS CLI

The Arista EOS CLI

Your Primary Interface for Device Management

Key Characteristics
  • Primary Tool: The CLI is the fundamental interface for all Arista device interactions.
  • Consistent & Intuitive: Designed for ease of learning and use, resembling other industry-standard CLIs.
  • Comprehensive Control: Enables monitoring, configuration, and troubleshooting of all device features.
Key Takeaway

Mastering the Arista EOS CLI is essential for effective network device management, providing a direct and powerful way to control your infrastructure.

Analogy: Network Control Panel

Imagine the Arista EOS CLI as the cockpit of an airplane. Just as a pilot uses various controls and instruments to fly, you use CLI commands to navigate, monitor, and configure your network switch. Each command is like a specific button or lever, allowing precise control over the device's functions. The consistent layout ensures that once you learn the basics, you can operate different 'models' of Arista switches with confidence.

Practical Relevance

From initial setup to advanced troubleshooting, the CLI is indispensable. It's where you'll spend most of your time interacting with Arista devices, making proficiency a core skill for network engineers.

Common Misconception

Some might think a GUI is always easier. While GUIs exist, the CLI offers granular control, automation capabilities, and is often the only access method during critical network failures or initial deployments.

screens.title: Understanding CLI Operational Modes
screens.narratorSegment: The Arista EOS CLI operates with a hierarchical structure, which means that the commands available to you change depending on your current operational mode. This design is intentional, helping to prevent accidental configuration changes and ensuring that you only have access to the commands relevant to your current task. When you first log into an Arista switch, you'll typically find yourself in what's called User EXEC mode. This mode is characterized by a simple greater-than symbol, like a right angle bracket, as its prompt. In User EXEC mode, your command options are very limited, primarily focused on basic monitoring and diagnostic commands. It's a safe, read-only environment, perfect for quick status checks without the risk of altering the device's configuration. Think of it as a guest account, where you can look around but not make any changes. Understanding this hierarchical structure is fundamental because it dictates your capabilities and guides your navigation through the CLI. You can't configure an interface from User EXEC mode, for example, because those commands simply aren't available there. In practical terms, a hierarchical approach to device interaction. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 2›Chapter 1›CLI Operational Modes

Understanding CLI Operational Modes

A Hierarchical Approach to Device Interaction

CLI Mode Hierarchy
User EXEC ModePrompt: Switch>Limited monitoring & diagnostics
Privileged EXEC ModePrompt: Switch#Full monitoring, gateway to config
Global Configuration ModePrompt: Switch(config)#System-wide settings
Specific Configuration ModesPrompt: Switch(config-if)#, etc.Interface, VLAN, Router settings
Purpose of Hierarchy

Prevents accidental configuration changes by limiting available commands based on privilege level.

User EXEC Mode (>)

Initial login mode with very limited commands, primarily for basic monitoring and diagnostics.

Key Takeaway

The EOS CLI uses a hierarchical mode structure to control command access, starting with the most restricted User EXEC mode.

screens.title: User EXEC vs. Privileged EXEC
screens.narratorSegment: Let's take a closer look at the first two crucial operational modes: User EXEC and Privileged EXEC. As we just discussed, User EXEC mode is your initial entry point, indicated by the greater-than symbol, like 'Switch>'. In this mode, you have a very restricted set of commands, primarily for basic monitoring and diagnostics. For example, you might use a command like 'show version' to check the software version, but you cannot make any configuration changes. It's a safe, read-only environment. To perform any significant monitoring or to begin making configuration changes, you must elevate your privileges to Privileged EXEC mode. This is achieved by simply typing the command 'enable' at the User EXEC prompt. If a password has been configured, you'll be prompted to enter it. Once successful, your prompt will change to a hash symbol, like 'Switch#'. In Privileged EXEC mode, you gain access to all 'show' commands, allowing for detailed device status checks, and crucially, you can now enter configuration modes. The distinction between these two modes is vital for security and operational control, ensuring that only authorized users with elevated privileges can make changes to the network device. Misunderstanding these modes can lead to frustration when commands don't work, or worse, accidental configuration changes.

keyIdea.title: Privilege Elevation
keyIdea.text: User EXEC mode (>) offers limited monitoring, while Privileged EXEC mode (#), accessed via 'enable', grants full monitoring and configuration access.

content.html:
Module 2›Chapter 1›User vs. Privileged EXEC
User EXEC Mode

Limited Access (Switch>)

  • Initial Login: First mode upon successful login.
  • Restricted Commands: Primarily basic monitoring and diagnostics.
  • Read-Only: No configuration changes possible.
Example Command
Switch>show version
Privileged EXEC Mode

Elevated Access (Switch#)

  • Access via enable: Elevates privileges from User EXEC.
  • Full Monitoring: Access to all show commands.
  • Configuration Gateway: Required to enter configuration modes.
Example Command
Switch>enable
Password:
Switch#show ip interface brief
Key Takeaway

Always start in User EXEC (>) for basic checks, then use 'enable' to transition to Privileged EXEC (#) for comprehensive monitoring and configuration access.

screens.title: Entering Global Configuration Mode
screens.narratorSegment: Once you're in Privileged EXEC mode, the next step for making any system-wide changes is to enter Global Configuration mode. This is your gateway to altering the fundamental behavior and settings of the Arista switch. You transition into this mode by typing the command 'configure terminal' at the Privileged EXEC prompt. Upon successful entry, your prompt will change to indicate that you are now in a configuration context, typically appearing as 'Switch(config)#'. In Global Configuration mode, you can apply settings that affect the entire device, such as defining the hostname, enabling or disabling various services, or setting global parameters like logging levels. For instance, if you want to change the name of your switch from 'Switch' to 'Core-Router-1', you would do that here. It's important to understand that commands entered in this mode have a broad impact across the device. If you try to configure an interface directly from Global Configuration mode, the CLI will tell you that the command is unrecognized because interface-specific commands belong in a different, more granular configuration context. This structured approach helps maintain order and prevents misconfigurations by ensuring commands are executed in their appropriate scope.

keyIdea.title: Global Settings Gateway
keyIdea.text: Global Configuration mode (config#), accessed via 'configure terminal', is where system-wide settings like hostname and services are applied.

content.html:
Module 2›Chapter 1›Global Configuration Mode

Entering Global Configuration Mode

Applying System-Wide Settings

Key Aspects
  • Access Command: Use configure terminal from Privileged EXEC mode.
  • Prompt: Indicated by (config)#.
  • Scope: Apply settings that affect the entire device (e.g., hostname, global services).
Key Takeaway

Global Configuration mode is essential for applying system-wide settings and is the necessary step before diving into more specific configuration contexts.

CLI Command Example
Switch#configure terminal
Switch(config)#hostname Core-Switch-1
Core-Switch-1(config)#
Why it Matters

This mode is the foundation for all device-level configurations, from basic identification to enabling critical network services. Without it, you cannot customize your switch's global behavior.

Common Mistake

Attempting to configure specific features (like an interface IP address) directly in Global Configuration mode. These require navigating to a more specific sub-mode.

screens.title: Diving into Specific Configuration Contexts
screens.narratorSegment: From Global Configuration mode, you can then navigate into even more specific configuration contexts to fine-tune particular aspects of your device. These sub-modes allow you to apply settings to individual components or services. For example, to configure an individual port on your switch, you would enter Interface Configuration mode, which changes your prompt to something like 'Switch(config-if)#'. Similarly, for defining VLAN properties, you'd go into VLAN Configuration mode, indicated by 'Switch(config-vlan)#', or for routing protocols, Router Configuration mode, with a prompt like 'Switch(config-router)#'. This granular approach ensures that commands are applied precisely where they are intended, preventing unintended side effects. To move back up the hierarchical structure, you have a couple of convenient commands. The 'exit' command will take you one step back, returning you to the previous mode. For instance, from Interface Configuration mode, 'exit' would bring you back to Global Configuration mode. If you want to jump directly back to Privileged EXEC mode from any configuration context, you can use the 'end' command or simply press 'Ctrl+Z'. These navigation commands are crucial for efficiently moving through the CLI and managing complex configurations.

keyIdea.title: Granular Configuration
keyIdea.text: Specific configuration modes (e.g., config-if#, config-vlan#) allow granular settings for components, with 'exit' to move up one level and 'end' or 'Ctrl+Z' to jump to Privileged EXEC.

content.html:
Module 2›Chapter 1›Specific Configuration Contexts

Diving into Specific Configuration Contexts

Interface, VLAN, and Router Modes

Interface Configuration

(config-if)#

Configure individual physical or logical ports (e.g., IP addresses, speed, duplex).

Switch(config)#interface Ethernet1
Switch(config-if)#ip address 10.0.0.1/24
VLAN Configuration

(config-vlan)#

Define properties for Virtual Local Area Networks (e.g., VLAN ID, name).

Switch(config)#vlan 10
Switch(config-vlan)#name Sales
Router Configuration

(config-router)#

Configure routing protocols (e.g., OSPF, BGP) and their parameters.

Switch(config)#router ospf 1
Switch(config-router)#network 10.0.0.0/8 area 0
Navigation Commands
  • exit: Moves up one level in the hierarchy.
  • end or Ctrl+Z: Jumps directly to Privileged EXEC mode.
Key Takeaway

Specific configuration modes enable granular control over device components, and efficient navigation with 'exit' and 'end' is crucial for managing complex configurations.

screens.title: Mastering CLI Navigation Aids
screens.narratorSegment: Navigating the Arista EOS CLI is made significantly easier and faster thanks to its powerful built-in help features. Your best friend in the CLI is the question mark character, '?'. Typing '?' at any prompt will immediately display a list of all available commands in your current operational mode. This is incredibly useful when you're unsure what commands are at your disposal or when exploring a new configuration context. But it gets even better: if you type a command followed by '?', the CLI will show you the next available parameters or options for that specific command. For example, typing 'show?' will list all the different 'show' commands, and if you then type 'show ip?', it will narrow down the options to only those related to IP. This context-sensitive help is a powerful learning tool and a time-saver. Additionally, EOS supports tab completion. If you start typing a command and then press the 'Tab' key, the CLI will either automatically complete the command for you if it's unique, or it will show you a list of possible completions if there are multiple options. This feature dramatically speeds up your typing, reduces errors, and helps you discover commands without having to type them out fully. Mastering these two features will make your CLI experience much more efficient and enjoyable.

keyIdea.text: Context-sensitive help ('?') and tab completion are essential CLI aids that accelerate command discovery and entry, reducing errors and boosting productivity.

content.html:
Module 2›Chapter 1›CLI Navigation Aids
Context-Sensitive Help

Using the '?' Character

  • List Commands: Typing ? shows all available commands in current mode.
  • Parameter Help: Command followed by ? shows next available options.
Example
Switch#show ?
Switch#show ip ?
Tab Completion

Using the 'Tab' Key

  • Auto-Complete: Completes unique commands or keywords.
  • Show Options: Displays possible completions if multiple exist.
  • Reduces Errors: Minimizes typos and speeds up command entry.
Example
Switch#conf<Tab> (completes to 'configure')
Switch#show int<Tab> (shows 'interface', 'interfaces', etc.)
Key Takeaway

Leverage '?' for discovering commands and parameters, and 'Tab' for efficient command completion to significantly enhance your CLI productivity.

screens.title: Connecting via the Console Port
screens.narratorSegment: When you first set up an Arista switch, or if you encounter a critical network issue that prevents remote access, the console port becomes your indispensable lifeline. This method is known as 'out-of-band' management because it doesn't rely on the network being operational. To connect, you'll use a serial cable, typically an RJ-45 to DB-9 or a USB-to-serial adapter, to link your computer directly to the switch's console port. On your computer, you'll need terminal emulation software, such as PuTTY, Tera Term, or SecureCRT, to establish the connection. It's crucial to configure your terminal emulator with the correct serial settings: 9600 baud rate, 8 data bits, no parity, and 1 stop bit, often abbreviated as 9600 8N1. A very common mistake here is using incorrect console settings, which will result in garbled, unreadable output or no connection at all. Always double-check these settings before attempting to connect. Console access is fundamental for initial device configuration, password recovery, or troubleshooting when the network infrastructure itself is down. It's the most reliable way to gain access to your switch, even in the most challenging scenarios.

Module 2›Chapter 1›Console Port Access

Connecting via the Console Port

Your Lifeline for Initial Setup and Recovery

Console Access Essentials
  • Out-of-Band: Independent of network status, crucial for initial setup or failures.
  • Physical Connection: Requires a serial cable (RJ-45 to DB-9 or USB-to-serial).
  • Terminal Software: Use PuTTY, Tera Term, or SecureCRT on your computer.
Key Takeaway

Console access is your most reliable method for initial switch setup and recovery, requiring a direct serial connection and specific terminal settings (9600 8N1).

Standard Console Settings
Baud Rate: 9600
Data Bits: 8
Parity: None
Stop Bits: 1
Common Mistake

Incorrect console settings (e.g., wrong baud rate) will lead to garbled output or no connection. Always verify 9600 8N1.

Real-World Scenario

During a new switch deployment, you'll use the console port to assign the initial IP address and enable SSH before it can be managed remotely over the network.

screens.title: Enabling Secure Shell (SSH) Access
screens.narratorSegment: While console access is vital for initial setup and emergencies, for day-to-day 'in-band' management, Secure Shell, or SSH, is the preferred method. SSH is a network protocol that provides a secure, encrypted channel for remote command-line access to your switch. This encryption is critical because it protects sensitive information, like your passwords and configuration commands, from being intercepted by unauthorized parties over the network. To enable SSH on an Arista switch, you first need to generate RSA cryptographic keys. These keys are fundamental for securing the SSH connection and are created in Global Configuration mode using the command 'crypto key generate rsa'. The switch will then generate a pair of public and private keys. After generating the keys, you must ensure the SSH service itself is enabled. This is done with the simple command 'service ssh' also in Global Configuration mode. Without these steps, SSH connections will fail, leaving your remote management insecure or impossible. It's a foundational security practice to always enable SSH with strong encryption for remote access, moving away from insecure protocols like Telnet. In practical terms, encrypted remote management for arista devices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 2›Chapter 1›Enabling SSH Access

Enabling Secure Shell (SSH) Access

Encrypted Remote Management for Arista Devices

Why SSH is Essential
  • Security: Encrypts all communication, protecting passwords and data.
  • In-Band Management: Access over the network, ideal for daily operations.
  • Standard Protocol: Widely used and trusted for remote access.
Key Takeaway

SSH is the secure, preferred method for remote Arista device management, requiring RSA key generation and service activation for encrypted communication.

SSH Configuration Steps
Step 1: Generate RSA Keys
Switch(config)#crypto key generate rsa

These cryptographic keys secure the SSH connection.

Step 2: Enable SSH Service
Switch(config)#service ssh

Activates the SSH daemon on the switch.

Security Warning

Never use Telnet for remote access; it sends credentials and data in plain text, making it highly vulnerable to eavesdropping.

screens.title: Setting Up Local User Accounts
screens.narratorSegment: To complete your secure access configuration, you must set up local user accounts on the Arista switch. SSH, by default, relies on valid user credentials for authentication, meaning you need a username and password defined on the device itself. This is a fundamental security practice to control who can log in and manage your network infrastructure. Let's walk through an example. From Privileged EXEC mode, you would first enter Global Configuration mode by typing 'configure terminal'. Then, to create a user, you use the 'username secret ' command. For instance, 'username admin secret AristaACE!' creates a user named 'admin' with the password 'AristaACE!'. It is absolutely crucial to use the 'secret' keyword here. The 'secret' keyword ensures that the password is encrypted using a strong hashing algorithm, typically SHA-256, when stored in the configuration. In contrast, if you were to use the 'password' keyword instead, the password would be stored in plain text, which is a significant security vulnerability. Always choose strong, complex passwords that combine uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers, and special characters. Forgetting the 'enable' password or your local user passwords can lock you out of your switch, potentially requiring a disruptive password recovery procedure. Therefore, securely documenting your credentials is paramount. This step ensures that only authenticated and authorized individuals can access your Arista devices, forming a critical layer of your network's security posture.

keyIdea.title: Local User Security
keyIdea.text: Configure local user accounts with 'username <user> secret <password>' in Global Configuration mode. Always use 'secret' for encrypted passwords and strong credentials to prevent unauthorized access.

content.html:
Module 2›Chapter 1›Local User Authentication

Setting Up Local User Accounts

Secure Administrative Access with username secret

Importance of Local Users
  • Authentication: SSH relies on these credentials for login.
  • Access Control: Defines who can manage the device.
  • Security Layer: Prevents unauthorized administrative access.
Key Takeaway

Always configure local user accounts with the 'secret' keyword for encrypted passwords and use strong credentials to ensure secure administrative access to your Arista switches.

Configuration Example
Switch#configure terminal
Switch(config)#username admin secret AristaACE!
Switch(config)#
'secret' vs. 'password'

Using secret encrypts the password in the configuration (e.g., SHA-256), while password stores it in plain text, creating a major security vulnerability.

Pro Tip: Password Recovery

Document all administrative credentials securely. Forgetting passwords can lead to a disruptive password recovery process.

The Arista Extensible Operating System, or EOS, Command Line Interface is the central hub for all your interactions with Arista switches. Think of it as the control panel for your network devices. Unlike some other operating systems that might have complex or inconsistent interfaces, EOS is designed to be highly intuitive and consistent. This means that once you learn the basic structure and commands, you'll find it easy to apply that knowledge across different Arista devices and features. This consistency is a huge advantage, especially for those who are already familiar with other industry-standard CLIs, as it significantly flattens the learning curve. The CLI allows you to perform a wide range of tasks, from simply checking the status of a port to configuring advanced routing protocols. It's the most direct and powerful way to manage your network infrastructure, making its mastery a fundamental skill for any network professional working with Arista equipment. Without a solid understanding of the CLI, effective management and troubleshooting of Arista devices would be nearly impossible. It's the language you speak to your network. The Arista EOS CLI operates with a hierarchical structure, which means that the commands available to you change depending on your current operational mode. This design is intentional, helping to prevent accidental configuration changes and ensuring that you only have access to the commands relevant to your current task. When you first log into an Arista switch, you'll typically find yourself in what's called User EXEC mode. This mode is characterized by a simple greater-than symbol, like a right angle bracket, as its prompt. In User EXEC mode, your command options are very limited, primarily focused on basic monitoring and diagnostic commands. It's a safe, read-only environment, perfect for quick status checks without the risk of altering the device's configuration. Think of it as a guest account, where you can look around but not make any changes. Understanding this hierarchical structure is fundamental because it dictates your capabilities and guides your navigation through the CLI. You can't configure an interface from User EXEC mode, for example, because those commands simply aren't available there. Understanding CLI Operational Modes means eos cli uses a hierarchical structure where available commands depend on the current operational mode, starting with limited user exec mode.. In practical terms, a hierarchical approach to device interaction. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's take a closer look at the first two crucial operational modes: User EXEC and Privileged EXEC. As we just discussed, User EXEC mode is your initial entry point, indicated by the greater-than symbol, like 'Switch>'. In this mode, you have a very restricted set of commands, primarily for basic monitoring and diagnostics. For example, you might use a command like 'show version' to check the software version, but you cannot make any configuration changes. It's a safe, read-only environment. To perform any significant monitoring or to begin making configuration changes, you must elevate your privileges to Privileged EXEC mode. This is achieved by simply typing the command 'enable' at the User EXEC prompt. If a password has been configured, you'll be prompted to enter it. Once successful, your prompt will change to a hash symbol, like 'Switch#'. In Privileged EXEC mode, you gain access to all 'show' commands, allowing for detailed device status checks, and crucially, you can now enter configuration modes. The distinction between these two modes is vital for security and operational control, ensuring that only authorized users with elevated privileges can make changes to the network device. Misunderstanding these modes can lead to frustration when commands don't work, or worse, accidental configuration changes.

Once you're in Privileged EXEC mode, the next step for making any system-wide changes is to enter Global Configuration mode. This is your gateway to altering the fundamental behavior and settings of the Arista switch. You transition into this mode by typing the command 'configure terminal' at the Privileged EXEC prompt. Upon successful entry, your prompt will change to indicate that you are now in a configuration context, typically appearing as 'Switch(config)#'. In Global Configuration mode, you can apply settings that affect the entire device, such as defining the hostname, enabling or disabling various services, or setting global parameters like logging levels. For instance, if you want to change the name of your switch from 'Switch' to 'Core-Router-1', you would do that here. It's important to understand that commands entered in this mode have a broad impact across the device. If you try to configure an interface directly from Global Configuration mode, the CLI will tell you that the command is unrecognized because interface-specific commands belong in a different, more granular configuration context. This structured approach helps maintain order and prevents misconfigurations by ensuring commands are executed in their appropriate scope.

From Global Configuration mode, you can then navigate into even more specific configuration contexts to fine-tune particular aspects of your device. These sub-modes allow you to apply settings to individual components or services. For example, to configure an individual port on your switch, you would enter Interface Configuration mode, which changes your prompt to something like 'Switch(config-if)#'. Similarly, for defining VLAN properties, you'd go into VLAN Configuration mode, indicated by 'Switch(config-vlan)#', or for routing protocols, Router Configuration mode, with a prompt like 'Switch(config-router)#'. This granular approach ensures that commands are applied precisely where they are intended, preventing unintended side effects. To move back up the hierarchical structure, you have a couple of convenient commands. The 'exit' command will take you one step back, returning you to the previous mode. For instance, from Interface Configuration mode, 'exit' would bring you back to Global Configuration mode. If you want to jump directly back to Privileged EXEC mode from any configuration context, you can use the 'end' command or simply press 'Ctrl+Z'. These navigation commands are crucial for efficiently moving through the CLI and managing complex configurations.

Navigating the Arista EOS CLI is made significantly easier and faster thanks to its powerful built-in help features. Your best friend in the CLI is the question mark character, '?'. Typing '?' at any prompt will immediately display a list of all available commands in your current operational mode. This is incredibly useful when you're unsure what commands are at your disposal or when exploring a new configuration context. But it gets even better: if you type a command followed by '?', the CLI will show you the next available parameters or options for that specific command. For example, typing 'show?' will list all the different 'show' commands, and if you then type 'show ip?', it will narrow down the options to only those related to IP. This context-sensitive help is a powerful learning tool and a time-saver. Additionally, EOS supports tab completion. If you start typing a command and then press the 'Tab' key, the CLI will either automatically complete the command for you if it's unique, or it will show you a list of possible completions if there are multiple options. This feature dramatically speeds up your typing, reduces errors, and helps you discover commands without having to type them out fully. Mastering these two features will make your CLI experience much more efficient and enjoyable.
